claims.text: AIOS splits the system into an application layer and a kernel layer, with the AIOS kernel isolating resources and LLM-specific services from agent applications.
The AIOS kernel provides scheduling, context management, memory management, storage management, and access control services for runtime agents.
In the AIOS kernel, agent queries are decomposed into sub execution units called AIOS syscalls to facilitate parallelism.
AIOS enforces isolation by preventing agents from directly manipulating resources, which also relieves agents of resource management.
AIOS encapsulates LLMs as 'cores', akin to CPU cores, through a unified interface that integrates diverse LLM endpoints.
AIOS centralizes all request queues in the scheduler module rather than distributing them across processing modules, so each module focuses only on execution.

AIOS implements two classic scheduling algorithms: First-In-First-Out (FIFO), which processes calls in arrival order but may increase waiting times for later requests, and Round Robin (RR), which cycles through calls in time slices.
AIOS's Round Robin scheduling depends on a context interrupt mechanism for LLM inference.
The AIOS context manager supports task interruption and resumption through snapshot and restoration, to stop long-running LLM inference syscalls from monopolizing resources.

The AIOS context manager has two approaches: text-based (for closed-source LLMs without logits access, saving decoded outputs) and logits-based (preserving the intermediate search tree structure for finer-grained state restoration).

AIOS has a memory manager for runtime agent data, a storage manager for persistent storage, a tool manager that loads tools and resolves call conflicts, and an access manager that implements access control and user intervention protocols.
AIOS schedulers derive from a BaseScheduler class, so FIFO, Round Robin and priority-based schedulers can be added without modifying existing implementations.
The AIOS SimpleContextManager enables preemptive multitasking by preserving LLM states across generation phases, with time-aware interruption.
AIOS reports up to 2.1x faster execution when serving agents built by various agent frameworks.

In an AIOS ablation (ReAct agents, HumanEval, Llama-3.1-8b), FIFO gave the shortest overall execution time, and RR ranked second in overall execution and average waiting time because context switching adds overhead.
In the same ablation, Round Robin performed better than FIFO on p90 agent waiting time because its fairer scheduling reduces the chance that later tasks wait longer.
AIOS docs describe the AIOS kernel as an abstraction on top of the OS kernel, with the AIOS SDK (Cerebrum) layered above it for developing and deploying agents.

AIOS docs describe a goal of letting different users' or developers' personal AIOS kernels coexist on one physical machine through virtualization, requiring scheduling and resource allocation across the virtual machines.
For computer-use agents, AIOS redesigns the Tool Manager to include a VM (Virtual Machine) Controller and an MCP Server, creating a sandboxed environment for safe interaction with computer systems.

The AIOS repository includes an experimental Rust rewrite (aios-rs) with trait definitions and placeholder implementations for context, memory, storage, tool, scheduler and LLM, which is not yet feature-parity.

Letta (MemGPT) treats the context window as the agent's RAM and uses three memory tiers: core memory (always in context), archival memory (vector-database long-term store), and recall memory (full conversation history).
In Letta/MemGPT the agent manages its own memory through function calls, using tools to edit core memory, search recall or archival memory, and insert archival entries.

Letta uses a heartbeat mechanism (request_heartbeat=true) so the agent can chain multiple tool calls in one turn without waiting for user input, and memory-pressure signals prompt it to summarize or archive when the context nears capacity.

Sandboxes isolate agent code execution from the host, but do not protect against context injection: an attacker controlling part of the agent's input can instruct it to run arbitrary commands inside the sandbox.

OS-level agent sandboxing restricts file system and network access using Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus socat on Linux/WSL2, and Microsoft MXC process containers on Windows, and covers child processes but not built-in non-process tools.
